lessons.title: Burst pressure
lessons.body: A GPU pool can have spare capacity on average and still run out during a burst. Requests queue when demand exceeds what the pool can serve.
lessons.post:
llm-d flow control, chapter 2: shared inference under burst pressure.

A GPU pool can have spare capacity on average and still run out during a traffic burst. With @_llm_d_ flow control enabled, excess requests are queued until capacity becomes available.

lessons.title: Shared traffic needs policies
lessons.body: Premium, standard, and batch requests share one pool. A lower admission ceiling for batch leaves headroom for higher-priority traffic. It does not preempt already-running jobs or guarantee latency.
lessons.post:
llm-d flow control, chapter 4: shared traffic needs policies.

Premium, standard, and batch requests share one pool. Admission is decided by the priority and fairness policies. For example, we can prevent starvation of premium traffic from long-running batch jobs by setting a lower admission ceiling for batch queues.

https://alexagriffith.github.io/flow-control-benchmarks/learn/flow-control-journey.html#page-3

lessons.title: Fairness within a priority band
lessons.body: Fairness policies choose a flow within the band: Round Robin, Global Strict, or Program-Aware. Round Robin takes turns across active flows. Global Strict compares queue heads using the ordering policy.
lessons.post:
llm-d flow control, chapter 5: fairness within a priority band.

Fairness policies choose a flow within the band: Round Robin, Global Strict, or Program-Aware. Round Robin takes turns across active flows. Global Strict compares queue heads using the ordering policy.

Ordering policies rank requests within each flow’s queue. Options are First-Come, First-Served (FCFS), Earliest Deadline First (EDF), or SLO Deadline.

This animation shows FCFS with Round Robin and Global Strict fairness policies.

https://alexagriffith.github.io/flow-control-benchmarks/learn/flow-control-journey.html#page-4

lessons.title: Request ordering
lessons.body: Compare First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) and Earliest Deadline First (EDF) within each queue, with Global Strict comparing queue heads across flows in the same priority band.
lessons.post:
llm-d flow control, chapter 5 continued: request ordering.

Ordering (within each queue):
(1) First come, first served (FCFS): Requests go in arrival order.
(2)  Earliest deadline first (EDF): Requests with the soonest deadline go first.

EDF calculates each deadline as the time the request entered flow control + its effective time-to-live (TTL).

Fairness (across queues in the same priority band): Global Strict compares queue heads using the ordering policy.

Try it yourself: https://alexagriffith.github.io/flow-control-benchmarks/learn/policy-lab/?fairness=strict&ordering=edf

lessons.title: Shared workloads: recap
lessons.body: A recap of burst pressure and admission ceilings in a shared pool. A lower batch ceiling leaves headroom for higher-priority requests; it does not guarantee their latency.
lessons.post:
llm-d flow control: a recap.

Different workloads have different SLOs. Chat may need fast responses, throughput for batch, and every tenant expects its work to make progress. With @_llm_d_ flow control, we can manage all of these workloads on the same GPUs.

Try it yourself: https://alexagriffith.github.io/flow-control-benchmarks/learn/flow-control-interactive.html#page-5

lessons.title: Grouping requests into queues
lessons.body: The Endpoint Picker uses the request’s objective to find its priority band, then its fairness ID to choose a queue within that band. Requests with the same priority and fairness ID share a queue.
lessons.post:
llm-d flow control, chapter 7: grouping requests into queues.

The Endpoint Picker gets the request’s priority from a defined InferenceObjective. That priority value maps to a flow control priority band that the request belongs to.

Within that band, the fairness ID (tenant) identifies the queue that the request belongs to. Requests with the same priority and fairness ID join the same queue.

Try it yourself: https://alexagriffith.github.io/flow-control-benchmarks/learn/flow-control-interactive.html#page-6
